correctness.rationale: The profile reduces exactly to one count and the number of 10 pairs. The two word weights in a common fiber depend only on its one count, giving the exact s^(2n) tilt to equal bias t=sqrt(pq)/s. The Canfield–Janson–Zeilberger local estimate applies with min(k,n-k) of order n, uniformly in the central binomial band. Replacing each inversion mass function by its lattice Gaussian changes its square-sum by at most the uniform error times the sum of the two masses, giving (2 sqrt(pi) sigma)^-1 to relative o(1), without summing errors over the full support. Off-band squared binomial masses are exponentially small. Parseval and expansion at the sole maximum give the composition factor (2 sqrt(pi n t(1-t)))^-1. Multiplying with sigma^2=k(n-k)(n+1)/12 gives sqrt(3)/(2 pi n^2 t(1-t)); t(1-t)=sqrt(pq(1-p)(1-q))/s². Direct enumeration through n=10 using (number of ones, sum of their positions) and rational exact weighting confirms the tilt at p=1/5, q=1/2, t=1/3, s²=9/10. The Gaussian binomial named in Step 3 is the unnormalized enumerator (the probability generating function divides by binomial(n,k)); the proof uses the correctly normalized mass throughout.
residual_risks: Fixed p,q strictly between 0 and 1; no boundary-uniform asymptotic. Finite enumeration is corroboration, not proof of the limit.

value.rationale: The sharp formula quantifies the collision risk of a standard finite subsequence profile, distinguishing quadratically many effective fair profiles from cubically many possible profiles. On unequal sources it gives both the exact exponential distinguishability rate and the polynomial correction, from the same statistic and without selecting special parameters. The exact tilted constant goes beyond a generic rate or repackaged fiber count.
residual_risks: This is an asymptotic for collisions, not a general information recovery theorem or a uniform estimate for near-degenerate sources.
